items.title: Hafta 607: Who pays for UPI? Is the UCC even ‘uniform’?
items.summary: This week on Hafta, Abhinandan Sekhri, Manisha Pande and Rinchen Norbu are joined by Anupam Manur, Professor of Economics at the Takshashila Institution, and Mihira Sood, Supreme Court lawyer specialising in women’s rights. The panel opens the discussion by examining the government’s decision to introduce a 0.4% fee on UPI merchant transactions above Rs 2,000, asking what the move means for a payment system that has become central to everyday transactions in India. Anupam Manur acknowledges that UPI generates wider economic benefits, but argues that the current model also creates a problem: who ultimately bears the cost of running the system? He explains that the cost of operating UPI is substantial, while the government subsidises only a portion of it. Manur says, “When UPI came about, India was miles ahead of the world in some sense. It was truly revolutionary.” But he argues that the costs leave new entrants with insufficient incentive, which has affected private-sector innovation. “Private players are just not incentivized to innovate.” The discussion then moves from the economics of UPI to the politics of its messaging. Abhinandan argues that the government has often reduced complicated policy questions to easily marketable slogans: “I think the problem is, like many things that Mr. Modi does ever since he’s come, let’s count his slogans. He’s a fantastic ad man.” The panel then turns to the BJP’s push for a Uniform Civil Code (UCC). Mihira offers a qualified position. She makes clear that she supports the idea of a UCC in principle, particularly as a route towards greater equality. But she distinguishes that principle from the particular version being discussed. She says, “What I have a problem with is this particular type of Uniform Civil Code because it is not based in secularism and it is not based in feminism.” Rinchen questions whether we should even call this a ‘uniform civil code’, given the carve-outs that exist for Scheduled Tribes in states like Uttarakhand, where the BJP has implemented its version of it. He also argues that the focus on polygamy in the UCC debate distracts from the larger issue of inheritance rights for women. “This whole bigamy, this whole polygamy thing is a red herring; it’s overstated,” he adds, while Mihira breaks down the real legal questions surrounding inheritance if the BJP actually cared about women’s rights. items.title: Delhi High Court stays JNU order imposing fine on students for smiling at protesters
items.summary: The Delhi High Court recently stayed Jawaharlal Nehru University's (JNU) order imposing ₹19,000 fine on certain students allegedly for merely smiling at certain protestors [Mr C Arjun & Ors v Jawaharlal Nehru University] . Justice Jasmeet Singh observed that the students' conduct "does not constitute any infraction which can be categorised as indiscipline of any sort". The Court observed that JNU's action strikes a blow at the students' fundamental rights and cannot be allowed. "I cannot lose sight of the fact that the petitioners are students in the respondent University and as a student, the right to express dissent/demonstrate and/or to express support by way of cheering for a demonstration, to my mind, constitutes a valuable right which cannot be allowed to be curbed or interdicted in any manner. The students/petitioners cannot be allowed to be punished for an act of such a nature," the Court observed. Justice Jasmeet Singh Delhi High Court The right to express dissent/demonstrate and/or to express support by way of cheering for a demonstration, to my mind, constitutes a valuable right which cannot be allowed to be curbed or interdicted in any manner. Justice Singh was hearing a petition filed by the students challenging a show cause notice dated January 15, 2026, issued by the office of the Chief Proctor, along with the office orders dated February 2, 2026 imposing fine on the students. The notice had later been upheld by subsequent appellate orders dated March 30. The show cause notice accused some students of aggressively shaking camera stands and vandalising the university's facial recognition technology (FRT) system. Three students were accused of encouraging and supporting the act by clapping and sloganeering during an incident on November 21, 2025. The petitioners denied any involvement, stating they were, at best, seen smiling at the protestors. After considering the case, the High Court found a prima facie case in the students' favour. Therefore, it stayed the University's order. Advocates Abhik Chimni, Moksha Sharma, Pranjal Abrol, Gurupal Singh, Ayan Dasgupta and Tushar Chandra represented the petitioner students. Senior Standing Counsel Ginny Jetley Rautray and advocate Arnav Tandon represented JNU. [Read Order]

items.title: Delhi HC orders CBI to issue Red Notice through Interpol to trace man making allegations against Indian courts
items.summary: The Delhi High Court has directed the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) to issue a Red Corner Notice through Interpol to trace an individual called Adeeshwar Singhal who is accused of making scandalous allegations against the judiciary [ Court On Its Own Motion Vs Adeeshwar Singhal ]. The Division Bench of Justice Navin Chawla and Justice Ravinder Dudeja passed the order to secure Singhal’s physical presence in court in suo motu contempt of court proceedings initiated against him. “We direct the Central Bureau of Investigation to issue a Red Corner Notice through INTERPOL against the respondent (Singhal) for securing his presence in compliance of our orders, including the non-bailable warrants (NBWs),” the Court directed. On September 18, Singhal joined the Court proceedings through video conference and engaged in disruptive conduct. "We will ensure that you come to court, don’t think we will leave you like this. You are making a mockery of the proceedings and making allegations. Either you come here or we will get you here," Justice Chawla warned. Justice Navin Chawla and Justice Ravinder Dudeja Standing Counsel Amit Tiwari informed the Court that Singhal had traveled from India to Italy in 2024 and has not returned since then. The Court was also informed that Singhal’s Indian passport has expired and his whereabouts are not known. “A Look Out Circular has also been issued but that might by itself not be sufficient to secure the presence inspite of the issuance of NBW,” the Court noted. A Delhi Police inspector told the Court that the IP address from which Singhal had joined the proceedings during a previous hearing in April was found to be in California at the United States of America. In view of this, the Court directed the Union Ministry of External Affairs to inform the concerned authorities in United States of America about the NBWs issued against Singhal, the expiry of his Indian Passport and also his IP Address. “He will now not use that passport. Wherever he is he is using some other identity,” the Court added. The Court also directed the Cyber Cell of the Delhi Police make inquiries regarding the IP address from which Singhal had joined the proceedings. The Court’s Registry was also directed to furnish the details of the IP address. The Court directed Singhal to appear in person on the next date of hearing. items.summary: We all carry our fair share of courtroom mishaps, particularly from the early years. While mistakes can happen at any stage of the litigation career, the shaking and trembling hits very differently to the newly robed, often accompanied by a strong conviction that the legal career is over and it’s time to relocate to another country. To celebrate these mandatory rites of passage, I polled my litigation circle and discovered these gems. 1. During my first year, I was sent to seek a simple passover before a Supreme Court bench with clear instructions to say “my senior is on his legs in another courtroom”. But of course, appearing before a Supreme Court bench, my overwhelm got the better of me and being painfully honest, I blurted out, “my senior is on his legs in the NCLT” . At this point, I was not aware of the unwritten rule of forum hierarchy. I got a well-deserved chewing out from my senior at this point. - 23 y/o advocate assisting a well sought after criminal lawyer in Delhi. 2. A towering 6ft+ young advocate dropped to one knee in open court at the Supreme Court to catch his senior’s whispered instructions. items.title: Forcing parties into mediation is always a bad idea: Justice Anup Jairam Bhambhani
items.summary: Forcing parties into mediation is always a bad idea and there is no universally right stage at which parties must attempt settlement, Delhi High Court judge Justice Anup Jairam Bhambhani said at the Commercial Mediation Conclave 2026. Justice Bhambhani said that the appropriate time for mediation depends on the nature of the dispute and whether the parties are genuinely willing to explore settlement. “I think what is or is not the right time to start mediation depends on the dispute. Forcing parties to mediation is always a bad idea. There are times when parties have been in litigation for very long, they have suffered the battle fatigue and all of that, the litigation fatigue and that's when it dawns on them that maybe we have been walking the wrong road .” He added that parties may become more receptive to mediation once the strengths and weaknesses of their respective cases become clearer. In disputes involving continuing commercial relationships, such as construction contracts, parties may also have practical reasons to preserve their association. Justice Bhambhani was speaking during a fireside chat on Mediation in Construction Disputes along with former Supreme Court judge Justice Hima Kohli. The session was moderated by Mehak Oberoi , author of Construction Mediation . On who should act as a mediator, Justice Bhambhani described mediation as a “standalone and extremely soft and specific skill”. He said that a mediator need not necessarily be a technical expert in the subject matter but must understand the “pathology” of the dispute. He added that technical assistance could be taken where required in specialised disputes such as patents or construction matters Justice Bhambhani agreed that government officers were often “petrified at taking a call” and suggested that high-powered committees of senior officers could support and approve settlements, reducing the fear attached to individual decision-making. Justice Kohli similarly stressed that being a judge and being a mediator required different approaches. “ Being a judge is one thing but being a mediator means wearing a different mantle and that mantle should not overlap with your authority as a judge .” She recalled undergoing mediation training herself while serving as a Supreme Court judge. Justice Kohli said officers may recognise that settlement is commercially sensible but still hesitate because of fears of audit objections, corruption allegations or career consequences. items.summary: Born in Amreli district of Gujarat, Justice Harsha Devani’s path to the judiciary was anything but conventional. After completing her schooling across Assam, Bihar and Gujarat, she earned her MSc in Microbiology before pursuing an LL.B. at Sir LA Shah Law College, Ahmedabad. She enrolled as an advocate with the Bar Council of Gujarat in 1992. She served as an assistant government pleader and additional public prosecutor, mastering constitutional, civil, and criminal law. Justice Devani was elevated to the Gujarat High Court bench on October 8, 2004 and confirmed as a permanent judge in 2007. She served with distinction until her retirement in March 2020. She continues to be a sought-after judge even long after retirement. Today, her deep expertise and humanity make her a revered voice in commercial dispute resolution. In this candid chat with Bar & Bench's Neha Joshi, Justice Devani offers sharp, pragmatic insights into India's evolving legal landscape. She critiques the operational realities of the Gujarat High Court Arbitration Centre, unpacks systemic flaws in senior advocate designations and evaluates Gujarat’s potential to emerge as a premier commercial arbitration hub. My father was advising my younger brother - who is 8 years younger than me and had just graduated as an engineer - to study law because he believed that knowledge of law was essential regardless of whether one practised or not. I happened to be standing there and asked my brother to get an admission form for me as well. That was the starting point of my legal career. items.title: A court’s search for assets and the cost to corporate certainty
items.summary: On August 31, 2026, in the long-running enforcement proceedings between Daiichi Sankyo and the Singh brothers, the Delhi High Court allowed three applications. In doing so, it drastically rewrote how strangers to an arbitral award may be treated under Indian law. By way of its order, the Court has appointed a forensic auditor to reconstruct the entire chain of dealings in the shares of Fortis Healthcare Limited (FHL) from May 24, 2016 onwards. Interestingly, FHL was not a party to the arbitration agreement, not a party to the award, not a judgment debtor and was not even a party to the assurances given to the Court by the judgement debtors - the Singh brothers and their holding companies. It is nevertheless the subject of the audit so directed, as are 17 banks and financial institutions. How the Court justifies this is worth examining closely. The direction for forensic audit, it holds, is "purely investigative in nature" and does not result "in the fastening of liability upon the entity whose affairs are directed to be examined". The characterisation is appealing: if the audit is only an enquiry, then no rights are affected and if no rights are affected, the stranger has nothing to complain about. That this enquiry may well pave the way for liability to be fastened later is a bridge the Court leaves for another day. Except that the order does not quite confine itself to investigation. Because the brothers served as chairman and vice-chairman of FHL, the Court holds that they were “the heart, soul and brain” of the company and that their knowledge was the company’s knowledge. On this footing, the assurances given by the brothers to protect the decretal amount are sought to be read as extending beyond their personal shareholding to cover the entirety of the promoter group’s stake in FHL. The Court’s predicament is not difficult to understand. A foreign award of considerable magnitude has remained substantially unsatisfied for close to a decade. Successive assurances given to the Court were breached by the brothers. The controlling stake in FHL was whittled down from over 70 per cent to less than 1 per cent while those assurances held. The Supreme Court has already found the brothers guilty of contempt. With no identifiable pool of assets in sight, the Court’s impulse to trace where the value has gone is entirely natural. items.summary: The Gujarat High Court on September 17 allowed Surat-based advocate to withdraw his plea seeking the quashing of a rape case against him. items.title: Israeli pharma giant Teva Israel wins tax battle before Delhi High Court against IT Department
items.summary: In a major victory for Israeli pharmaceutical company Teva Israel, the Delhi High Court has held that a ₹1,851 crore payment made by Ranbaxy Laboratories to Teva Israel under a settlement agreement is not taxable in India [Teva Pharma Vs Union of India]. By way of an order passed on September 15, a bench of Justices Dinesh Mehta and Vinod Kumar said the payment could not be taxed merely because it was made by an Indian company to a foreign entity. “ Mere payment by an Indian resident to a non-resident ipso facto does not constitute an income accruing or arising in India.The transaction neither falls within any of the specific deeming provisions under Section 5(2)(b) of the Act of 1961 nor of Section 9. In the absence of both, the jurisdictional foundation for issuance of notice under section 148 collapses, ” the Court held. Ranbaxy had already deducted tax before making payment to Teva. The refund of the amount to Teva would be subject to Teva USA and Teva Israel furnishing the guarantees directed by the Court. Justice Dinesh Mehta and Justice Vinod Kumar The case concerned Atorvastatin, a cholesterol-lowering medicine sold by Pfizer under the brand name Lipitor. Ranbaxy was the first company to apply for US regulatory approval to sell a generic version of the drug. It was consequently entitled to a 180-day period during which no other applicant for the generic drug could receive approval. However, there was initially uncertainty over whether Ranbaxy would receive final approval on time. In December 2010, Ranbaxy India, its US subsidiary and Teva USA entered into an agreement governing what would happen if Ranbaxy was unable to use its exclusivity. Under the agreement, Ranbaxy would selectively waive or relinquish its exclusivity in favour of Teva USA if Teva issued a valid “Ready Date Notice” after satisfying stipulated conditions concerning regulatory approval and its readiness to launch the drug. Teva USA issued such a notice on November 23, 2011. Ranbaxy disputed its validity. Teva USA then instituted proceedings before a US court seeking enforcement of the agreement. The dispute was settled with effect from November 30, 2011, the same day on which Ranbaxy received final approval for its generic drug. Ranbaxy began selling Atorvastatin in the United States the following day. Ranbaxy earned around $700 million in profits during the six-month exclusivity period. items.title: Karnataka HC stays circulars deferring revised minimum wages for outsourced, contract workers
items.summary: The Karnataka High Court on Friday stayed the operation of circulars that direct various authorities to withhold the implementation of revised minimum wages for outsourced and contract employees [ All India Trade Union Congress & others v. items.title: Delhi High Court pulls up Delhi government over shortage of doctors, qualified staff in city hospitals
items.summary: The Delhi High Court on Friday pulled up the Delhi government for not recruiting the necessary qualified doctors and staff at government hospitals. A bench of Justice Prathiba M Singh and Justice Manmeet Pritam Singh Arora noted that due to the inadequate recruitment of qualified staff, valuable equipment was also going unused. "There are no technicians running these equipments. The court is completely dissatisfied with the report placed on record. The hospitals are facing enormous difficulty in recruiting the necessary doctors and the staff. There is no uniform HR policy of the Delhi Government," the Court said. Justice Prathiba M Singh and Justice Manmeet Pritam Singh Arora The Court went on to observe, “ Judges will come, judges will go, but the hospitals have to function ." The Court was hearing a suo motu case in which it routinely monitors healthcare services in the city's government hospitals. On August 7 , the Court had expressed shock after being informed that 400 ventilators and 910 oxygen concentrators are lying unused at Guru Teg Bahadur (GTB) Hospital. The Court, in response, had directed the Secretary of the Department of Health and Family Welfare under Delhi government to hold a meeting regarding the recruitment of staff for operating such equipment. In yesterday's hearing of the matter, the Court expressed dissatisfaction over the poor progress made since then. "It does not appear that after the meeting had taken place on August 13, any recruitment has happened," the Court said. It has now directed the Secretary of the Health Department to hold a fresh meeting with each hospital on the issue of recruitment. items.title: Karnataka High Court quashes criminal case against Pearson Education's former in-house counsel
items.summary: The Karnataka High Court has quashed criminal proceedings against former in-house legal counsel of Pearson Education/ Dorling Kindersley (India) Pvt Ltd, Prashant Kumar Joshi [Prashant Kumar Joshi v State of Karnataka]. By way of an order passed on September 11, Justice HP Sandesh quashed the criminal proceedings against Joshi in a case concerning legal metrology violations by Pearson Education. The Court said that Joshi was not a nominated personnel of the company (under Section 49 of the Legal Metrology Act), responsible for the company's business and conduct. The Court ruled that criminalising the former in-house counsel without the company being a party to the proceedings, would amount to an abuse of process of law. "Nothing is stated in the complaint that this petitioner was in charge of the affairs of the company and he being shown as General Manager (Legal), the question of initiating the criminal prosecution against this petitioner is nothing but an abuse of process, which amounts to miscarriage of justice," the order said. Justice HP Sandesh The case stemmed from a private complaint was filed against Joshi when he was working with Pearson Education as a General Manager (Legal). In January 2012, the Inspector of Legal Metrology had found a pre-packed packaged Engineering Drawing textbook published by Pearson Education that did not mention the manufacturer's name and address, maximum retail price, net contents of the package, consumer care telephone number, and e-mail address. The omission of the details were alleged violations under the Legal Metrology Act, 2009 and the Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011. The Court relied on the legal principle of corporate liability provided under the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1938 and interpreted in Supreme Court precedents to hold the prosecution of Pearson's former counsel to be unsustainable without arraigning the company as a party. Advocates Shrikara PK and Ganapati Hegde appeared for Pearson's former in-house counsel. High Court Government Pleader M Divakar Madhu appeared for the State. items.title: Home guard arrested after video shows him beating, dragging woman by hair in Hyderabad
items.summary: Follow TNM's WhatsApp channel for news updates and story links. A home guard on deputation to the Railway Protection Force (RPF) was arrested after visuals of him beating a woman and dragging her by her hair across the street went viral on social media. The incident took place on the evening of Friday, September 18, outside Hyderabad’s Hafeezpet Railway station. The home guard, Anand, has also been dismissed from service. In the FIR registered against Anand at Miyapur police station, the complainant, head constable S Gopal, stated that he got to know about the assault while he was out on patrol. Gopal was accompanied by Special Police Officer (SPO) Rajeshwar Reddy. Gopal said in his complaint that they made enquiries after learning about the assault and came to know that Anand was involved. However, they were unable to trace the woman who was allegedly assaulted. The case against Anand was registered under Sections 74 (punishes assault or the use of criminal force against a woman with the intent to outrage her modesty) and 118(1) (voluntarily causing bodily hurt using dangerous weapons or hazardous means) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS). Visuals of the assault went viral on social media, drawing widespread outrage over the home guard’s behaviour. Telangana Director General of Police (DGP) CV Anand described the incident as one that “cannot be forgiven”. “Such behaviour by our staff, whatever be the rank and whatever be the provocation, cannot be forgiven,” he said. “It is abominable and in total disregard of all instructions and training. Enquiry has revealed that this home guard is on deputation to the Railway Police force and is not with the local police. items.title: Telangana sets up fast-track panel for disputes on land prohibited under Registration Act
items.summary: The Telangana government, on September 18, announced the constitution of a high-level committee to address land disputes involving section 22A of the Registration Act (1908) and to expedite pending cases. The move comes two days after Telangana Chief Minister Revanth Reddy's promise in the Assembly to look into concerns. The announcement was made by Revenue Minister Ponguleti Srinivas Reddy during the September 18 Assembly session. A three-member panel will be headed by Chief Commissioner of Land Administration (CCLA) DS Lokesh Kumar. Law Secretary B Papi Reddy and Inspector General of Registration and Stamps Rajiv Gandhi Hanumanthu will be its members. The committee has been asked to examine cases involving properties on the prohibited list and work towards resolving the identified issues within a month. The government has also begun implementing measures announced under the CM’s 12-point action plan on land-related matters. Section 22A of the Registration Act gives the state government the power to put certain lands (like government, assigned, forest and waqf lands) on a prohibited list. During past land record updates, alleged administrative and mapping errors wrongly placed thousands of acres of genuine private patta lands and entire residential colonies into the 22A prohibited list. While the opposition Bharat Rashtra Samithi (BRS) has accused the state government of manufacturing or failing to fix these issues in a bid for personal monetary gain and kickbacks, the state government claims the vast majority of the 98+ lakh restricted acres are public, forest, and endowment assets, with only a few lakh acres tied to private disputes. In the LB Nagar area, authorities have been directed to dispose of applications submitted under GO Ms No 118 within a month. Nearly 9,800 applications have been submitted in the constituency. The process is subject to court orders wherever applicable. Regularisation is scheduled to begin on September 19. Eligible properties are to be removed from the Section 22A prohibited list after the process is completed. The government is also preparing to address registration issues involving layouts and colonies that received approvals from agencies such as the Hyderabad Metropolitan Development Authority (HMDA), Greater Hyderabad Municipal Corporation (GHMC) and Directorate of Town & Country Planning (DTCP) but were subsequently affected by their inclusion in the Section 22A list. items.title: Tulu is now an additional official language in Karnataka
items.summary: Karnataka’s Cabinet has approved Tulu as an additional language for administrative purposes in Dakshina Kannada and Udupi. The move will allow government offices in the two districts to use Tulu for administrative work, with the government allocating Rs 82 lakh annually for translation, training and related activities. The decision comes after years of demands from Tulu organisations for greater recognition, including inclusion in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution. The move also comes against the backdrop of Tulu’s cultural and political significance in coastal Karnataka. Pro-Kannada organisations, including Karnataka Rakshana Vedike, have also supported the recognition of Tulu while calling for the development of both languages.

The Department of Collegiate Education issued the detailed safety guidelines on September 11 and directed principals to brief students about the restrictions before the start of a tour. Faculty members have also been asked to closely monitor students during excursions. According to the Times of India report , colleges must obtain written approval from the department before organising an educational tour. They must also submit undertakings from students and formal consent from parents along with the tour proposal. Once a tour is approved, its itinerary cannot be changed. Students cannot be taken to locations that are not included in the approved plan. The department has also advised colleges against organising educational tours during the monsoon season. For tours involving potentially risky locations such as rivers, seas, waterfalls, dense forests or steep hills, colleges have been directed to make safety arrangements in advance. If trekking or swimming is included in the itinerary, students can participate only when certified experts are part of the team and local safety clearances have been obtained. Local police officers must also be informed about the tour. Colleges have to provide the police with details of the trip and its itinerary. At least one permanent lecturer must accompany every tour. Students cannot be taken on excursions supervised only by guest lecturers. The number of teaching staff accompanying a tour has been capped at four. The team must include two female lecturers and one Group D employee.

items.title: IIT-Madras Research Park hosts 2-day conference on dementia, support for caregivers
items.summary: The Tamil Nadu government will work to make the state "dementia friendly” and treat the condition as a public health priority, Health and Family Welfare Minister KG Arun Raj announced on September 18. The Minister was speaking at the Dementia Conference (DemCon 2026) organised by the Dementia India Alliance (DIA). The conference was held at the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Madras Research Park on September 18 and 19. DIA is a national NGO that works with persons with dementia and their family caregivers. The organisation focuses on building awareness, early identification, diagnosis, care and support, caregiver capacity building, and pushes for inclusive policy making. DemCon was organised in collaboration with Tamil Nadu’s Department of Health and Family Welfare, Schizophrenia Research Foundation (SCARF), Heritage Foundation, and Kshetra Assisted Living by Heritage ElderCare Services. The conference is also in association with the National Institute of Mental Health Neuro Sciences (NIMHANS), the Global Brain Health Institute (GBHI), the Institute of Human Behaviour and Allied Sciences (IHBAS), and the Centre for Brain Session. The DIA’s State Dementia Action Plan, based on discussions held at the conference with stakeholders, was also presented to Minister Arun. The two-day conference covered a range of subjects. Panels discussed concerns such as recent findings on dementia, early biomarkers, diversity in symptoms, varieties of care, public policy, and building support frameworks for caregivers. Close to 10 lakh people in Tamil Nadu may live with dementia by 2036, according to projections, DIA said. At present, many do not have a formal diagnosis, and their families are forced to manage the condition without any trained support, they added. Speaking to TNM, Ramani Sundaram, clinical neuroscientist and executive director of DIA, said, “One of the largest challenges is that people have a lack of awareness. Most of the time, the signs and symptoms of dementia are passed off as signs of old age.” Stigma around mental health is another barrier, she said. “This is especially true among the elderly. Eight months after the CBI constituted SIT ruled out the presence of animal fat in the Tirumala ghee adulteration case, the Enforcement Directorate (ED) on Friday, September 18 named six adulterants and various other chemicals which were used to adulterate ghee. The ED mad no mention of animal fats being an adulterant. In a press note issued by the ED, the probe agency stated that it had arrested Kailash Chand Mangla, promoter of Sukriti Foods Pvt Ltd, in connection with the alleged adulteration and fraudulent supply of ghee to the Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams (TTD). As part of its probe, ED also said that adulterated ghee was allegedly manufactured using ‘refined palm oil, palm kernel oil, palmolein, and various chemicals including MG-90, monoglycerides, Myvacet soft 400, and Acetic Acid Esther.” In September 2024, Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister Chandrababu Naidu, Deputy CM Pawan Kalyan and Human Resource Development minister Nara Lokesh had claimed that lab reports showed the ghee used to prepare the Tirupati laddus during the previous YSR Congress Party (YSRCP) government contained animal fat, including beef tallow and fish oil. This allegation triggered widespread media coverage amid accusations of hurt religious sentiments. The product was allegedly passed off as “Agmark Special Grade cow ghee” and supplied to the TTD for preparing the Tirumala laddu prasadam. The agency has estimated the value of the ghee supplied between 2019 and 2024 at around Rs 230 crore. Of this, ghee worth approximately Rs 96 crore was allegedly manufactured by Mangla, the ED said. Mangla was arrested by the ED’s Hyderabad zonal office on Thursday, September 17, under Section 19 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), 2002. He was subsequently produced before the PMLA Special Court in Visakhapatnam, which remanded him to judicial custody. Mangla has been accused of facilitating the procurement of adulterants and manufacturing the product at his factory premises. The ED has also alleged that he helped coordinate supplies through several entities, including Sri Vyshnavi Dairy Specialities Pvt. Ltd., Malganga Milk & Agro Products Pvt. Ltd. and A.R. Dairy Foods Pvt. Ltd.
